args.text: Utterson and Enfield take their Sunday walk down a by-street.
Enfield points his cane at a sinister door and asks Utterson if he ever remarked it.
Enfield says the door is connected with a very odd story.
The man tramples over the girl's body and leaves her screaming.
Enfield collars the man and brings him back to the group around the child.
The doctor turns sick and white with desire to kill the prisoner.
They threaten scandal and force the man to pay a hundred pounds.
The man leads them to the door, unlocks it, and returns with gold and a cheque.
The man offers to stay until the banks open and cash the cheque himself.
They spend the night in Enfield's chambers and go to the bank next day.
Enfield presents the cheque believing it a forgery, but it proves genuine.
Enfield calls the door place Black Mail House and muses.
Utterson asks if the cheque drawer lives there.
Enfield says he noticed the drawer's address in some square.
Enfield explains his rule of not asking questions.
Enfield describes the door house: no other door, clean shut windows, smoking chimney.
Utterson asks the name of the man who walked over the child.
Enfield names the man as Hyde.
Enfield describes Hyde as deformed and detestable.
Utterson asks if Hyde used a key.
Utterson says he already knows the other party's name.
Enfield confirms Hyde still has the key and used it a week ago.
Enfield and Utterson agree never to refer to the matter again.
